prompt: Explain to a teammate why every one of these three platforms uses an asynchronous submit/queue/stream loop instead of a plain request that returns the generated image.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) inference is slow (seconds to minutes) so holding an HTTP request open blocks a connection and doesn't scale; (2) a queue decouples the fast stateless submit tier from the slow GPU worker so the API never sits on a GPU; (3) the result comes back on a separate channel (poll/SSE/WS) — the async request-reply pattern. Bonus: naming it as Queue-Based Load Leveling / async request-reply, a pattern that transfers to any stack.
source_quote: the submit call returns a job handle immediately, and the result comes back later over a separate channel

sources.label: AWS Prescriptive Guidance — gen-AI inference architecture

prompt: Name the nine stages of the universal serving loop in order, and say which single edge makes it a loop rather than a straight pipeline.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) client, auth, submit, queue, scale-to-zero GPU worker, weight staging, infer, output store, progress stream — in that order; (2) the back-edge is the progress stream returning status/result to the client on a channel the submit call never held open. Bonus: that the submit call returned a job handle before the result existed, which is what the back-edge later resolves.
source_quote: the result returns to the caller on a channel the submit call never held open

prompt: A colleague is designing a serving API and writes: 'the /generate endpoint runs the model and returns the image.' Using the loop, what did they collapse, and what are the submit tier's only two jobs?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) they fused the submit stage and the worker stage into one synchronous call, putting GPU work in the stateless API tier; (2) the submit API's only jobs are validate and enqueue, returning a job id immediately; (3) the GPU work belongs to a queue-fed worker pool and the result comes back on a separate progress channel. Bonus: under concurrency the second request has no free worker and times out because there is no queue to absorb the burst.
source_quote: a stateless call that validates and enqueues only, then returns a job id. It must not do GPU work in-process.

prompt: You need a progress channel for a long image job. Given the choices in this lesson, which transport is the correct default for one-way progress, and when would you upgrade to a WebSocket?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) SSE (Server-Sent Events) is the correct default for one-way server-to-client progress — plain HTTP with automatic reconnection; (2) upgrade to a WebSocket only when the client also needs to send messages mid-job (bidirectional); (3) polling is the most robust stateless fallback. Bonus: using a WebSocket for one-way progress is over-engineering, and polling over a WebSocket misuses the socket.
source_quote: use SSE for one-way progress; upgrade to WebSocket only when the client talks back

prompt: A design review diagram shows all three platforms as an identical seven boxes. Name two of the three honest asymmetries this hides, and why each matters.
expected_answer: Should mention any two of: (1) REDACTED's Bedrock path has no platform-owned worker/queue — the managed service owns that box, so 'someone else's worker'; (2) REDACTED's auth is AWS-account trust, not a per-request authorizer, so don't draw a Cognito-style gate; (3) REDACTED's worker is a warm-pod floor (KEDA minReplicaCount 1) because GPU cold start is 3-4 min, not literal zero. Bonus: that a too-clean diagram over-claims and the source explicitly corrects each of these.
section_heading: Three places the loop must stay honest
source_section: Three places the loop must stay honest

prompt: Someone stores generated images directly in the SQS/DynamoDB queue message to 'keep it simple.' Debug this: what breaks, and what is the queue actually for?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) the queue is a broker for references and short control messages, not a result store — large artifacts blow past message-size limits and bloat the queue; (2) results belong in a separate object store (S3), and inputs pass as S3 references, not inline bytes; (3) keeping broker and result store separate is the established rule. Bonus: REDACTED enforces exactly this by requiring image/mesh inputs as S3 references.
section_heading: Two ways to break the loop
source_section: Two ways to break the loop
source_quote: Keep the queue (SQS / DynamoDB / Redis) and the result backend (S3) separate.
